title: A Well for the Hymn
premise: Mara Okafor hosts the graveyard-shift call-in show 'The Hymn Line' in the dying town of Corrick's Bend, where last week's dead keep phoning in with calm, specific requests. When a county excavation crew breaches a door sealed from the inside beneath the old chapel well, the calls turn urgent: something taken in 1974 must be returned before the solstice, or the town's living will join its dialing dead. Mara, a documented orphan of that same year, discovers he was the thing taken—a baby swapped to hide a murder committed by the town's founding families. With a disgraced archivist and the ghost-voiced girl who first called him, Mara chooses justice over anonymity, publicly reading the 1974 names on air and carrying the stolen ledger back down the well. The door closes behind him at dawn; the calls stop; but every radio in Corrick's Bend now plays one faint hymn, and Mara's voice is the one singing it.
about_author: Xanthe Galloway is the pen name of a former night-shift emergency dispatcher who spent six years answering phones in a town smaller than its cemetery. They write horror about switchboards, small towns, and the terrible intimacy of voices you recognize.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. During his lonely overnight broadcast, a caller named Ruth asks him to tell her sister she forgave her—then Mara learns Ruth was buried Tuesday. He tapes the call, tells no one, and feels both terrified and, shamefully, less alone. Beat: eerie wonder cracking open a guarded life.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. He builds a logbook of the dead callers: times, numbers, requests. His station manager Del warns him off; listener Odile Vasseur, an excommunicated parish archivist, recognizes the pattern from 1974 records she was ordered to burn. Beat: obsession hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The county crew digging the flood-relief channel beside the ruined chapel hits masonry forty feet down. Odile arrives uninvited and sees, before they cover it again, a door—oak, iron-banded, scratched raw on the inside. Beat: dread arriving ahead of understanding.

chapters.title: Sealed from Within
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The foreman, Bo Tackett, comes on air drunk, describing the hinges fused by heat from the inside. That night the dead callers stop asking favors and start repeating one phrase: 'Bring back what you took.' Beat: the mystery acquires a demand.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In the diocesan basement, Odile finds the mutilated parish register: seven baptisms struck out in August 1974, including one infant recorded as 'returned.' She photographs everything and mails copies to herself. Beat: the past has fingerprints.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Called First
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A teenage caller, Wren, admits she phoned the show three weeks ago pretending to be her dead mother—as a joke, until the voice answered back using things only her mother knew. Mara realizes the phenomenon predates the excavation. Beat: complicity and alliance.

chapters.title: Tackett's Confession
chapters.summary: Bo's POV. Bo's grandfather helped seal the door in '74 after 'the Well family business went wrong,' and Bo has dreamed of scratching sounds ever since. He gives Mara his grandfather's key ring and begs him to go public. Beat: inherited guilt seeking absolution.

chapters.title: Static Hymn
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren teaches Mara the hymn the callers hum between sentences; when she sings it alone in her truck, every streetlight on Route 9 dies in sequence behind her. Her dead mother's voice says: 'You shouldn't have learned it yet.' Beat: wonder curdling to danger.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Cross-referencing the struck-out baptisms, Odile maps them to seven surnames still holding every bank seat, deed, and judgeship in the county—including Tackett, and including 'Okafor' entered in a different hand. Beat: the conspiracy has a census.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Someone ransacks the station and steals his logbook. Mara realizes the families have always known what he is—and that his quiet life was arranged, maintained, paid for. Beat: the found invisibility revealed as a cage.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The 1974 truth surfaces: the Well family's last daughter bore a child by a Black laborer murdered to conceal it; the baby—Mara—was swapped into an orphanage pipeline, and the mother was sealed alive in the well-chapel with the evidence. Beat: grief and fury braided together.

chapters.title: Solstice Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The dead callers give him a countdown: nine days. Living townsfolk begin dreaming of scratching. Del quits rather than help; the sheriff, a founding-family name, serves Mara a cease-and-desist. Beat: institutions choose the door over the truth.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Bo's POV. Bo surrenders his grandfather's ledger—payments, dates, the murder order signed by all seven patriarchs. Two of the seven descendant families, horrified, quietly offer testimony. Beat: justice assembling itself outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. On air, Mara reads the ledger aloud, name by name, for two hours while the families' lawyer screams in the lobby. Half the town listens; half burns effigies. The dead callers, for the first time, applaud—static like slow hands. Beat: defiant catharsis.

chapters.title: Retaliation
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The station tower is toppled; Odile's archive room floods under suspicious circumstances; Bo is hospitalized by men wearing county jackets. Wren hides the ledger copies inside her mother's grave goods. Beat: the cost of being seen.

chapters.title: Down the Access Road
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. With three days left, Mara, Odile, and Wren drive to the excavation at night and find the crew's shoring already collapsed inward—the door standing exposed, warm to the touch, breathing. Beat: threshold terror.

chapters.title: The Door Opens Inward
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara speaks his mother's recovered name—Adaeze Well—to the door, and it unlocks from the inside. What waits isn't a monster but a kept place: her bones, her scratched hymns, her unfinished letter naming her son. Beat: devastating tenderness.

chapters.title: Return
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. They carry the ledger, the register pages, and Adaeze's remains up into moonlight and lay them in consecrated ground as the solstice sun rises. The seven families arrive to stop it and find the whole listening town already there, silent. Beat: communal reckoning.

chapters.title: The Last Call
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. At dawn the board lights one final time: Adaeze's voice, whole and unhurried, telling him she heard every broadcast, that documentation was her prayer too, and that he may put the headphones down now. Beat: blessing and release.

chapters.title: After the Verdict
chapters.summary: Bo's POV. Indictments land; two families settle, one flees, one patriarch hangs himself in the chapel ruins. Bo testifies with his grandfather's key ring on the stand. Justice is slow, partial, real. Beat: bitter, necessary accounting.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Months later: Odile reopens the archive as a public memorial; Bo coaches Wren's softball team; Wren's mother's grave gets fresh flowers from strangers. Wren stops calling the dead and starts calling Mara, collect, just to talk. Beat: warmth earned through ruin.

chapters.title: A Well for the Hymn
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The station runs a new sign-off: silence, then the hymn, sung faintly by a voice listeners swear is Mara's though he never opens his mouth on air. He logs it, dates it, and writes: 'Some doors close so a choir can open.' Beat: haunted peace.
